lede: A sickly vicar's son from the Isle of Wight who drew a flea the size of a dinner plate, named the cell, worked out the law of springs, helped rebuild London after the Great Fire, and spent his last decades quarrelling with Isaac Newton.

ps: Robert Hooke was born at Freshwater on the Isle of Wight on 18 July 1635. His father, John Hooke, was the curate of the parish church.

He was the Royal Society's first Curator of Experiments, paid to show the Fellows new experiments at almost every meeting. His book Micrographia (1665) revealed the world under the microscope and gave biology the word 'cell'.

He was also an astronomer, an inventor of instruments and, after the Great Fire of 1666, one of the surveyors and architects who rebuilt London. He died in his rooms at Gresham College, London, on 3 March 1703, aged 67.
He was a weak child and was not expected to live. Too ill for regular school, he spent his time making things: a wooden clock that worked, and a model warship that fired tiny guns.

His father died in 1648, leaving him a small inheritance. He went to London, was briefly apprenticed to the portrait painter Peter Lely, then entered Westminster School, where the headmaster Richard Busby took him into his house.

Around 1653 he went to Christ Church, Oxford, as a chorister and servant to pay his way. There he joined a group of brilliant experimenters, and worked as an assistant to the physician Thomas Willis and then to Robert Boyle.
The air pump, 1658 to 1659. For Boyle he designed and built an improved air pump, which made Boyle's experiments on air pressure possible. The work behind Boyle's law owes much to Hooke's hands.
Curator of Experiments, 1662. The new Royal Society, founded in 1660, hired him to run its demonstrations. He became a Fellow in 1663.

Micrographia, January 1665. Published by the Royal Society, with large, beautiful engravings from his own drawings. Samuel Pepys sat up until two in the morning reading it and called it 'the most ingenious book that ever I read'.
Gresham College, 1665. He became Professor of Geometry at Gresham College in the City of London and lived there for the rest of his life.

The Great Fire, 1666. The fire burned for four days in September and destroyed most of the old City. Hooke offered a plan for rebuilding, and became one of the City's surveyors, measuring plots, settling disputes and checking new buildings. He worked closely with his friend Christopher Wren for years.

Springs, 1676 to 1678. He published his law of elasticity first as a Latin anagram, ceiiinosssttuv, then explained it in 1678: ut tensio, sic vis, 'as the extension, so the force'. A spring stretches in step with the load.

Newton, 1679 to 1687. In letters in 1679 he asked Isaac Newton how a planet would move under a pull falling off with distance. In 1684 he claimed he had proved the inverse square law of gravity but did not show the proof. When Newton's Principia appeared in 1687, Hooke said he deserved credit. Newton angrily removed several references to Hooke from the book.
Last years, 1690s to 1703. He grew ill and bent, kept a detailed diary, and lived among his books and instruments. He left a large sum of money and no will.

Micrographia (1665): the eye of a fly, the point of a needle, mould, a louse holding a hair, and a flea drawn on a fold-out sheet. Looking at a thin slice of cork he saw tiny boxes and called them cells, after the small rooms of monks.
Hooke's law, the rule for springs that still underlies the design of scales, watches and buildings.
Instruments: the improved air pump, better microscopes, a wheel barometer, and work on balance springs for pocket watches, which led to a priority quarrel with Christiaan Huygens.
Ideas ahead of their time: that fossils were remains of living things and showed that the earth had changed, that light might be a wave, and that gravity could be a pull reaching between the planets.

Buildings: the Royal College of Physicians, the new Bethlem Hospital at Moorfields (1676), and, with Wren, the Monument to the Great Fire (1671 to 1677), a column that was also meant as a giant scientific instrument.
Robert Boyle (1627 to 1691), the rich chemist who employed him and remained a friend and patron.
Christopher Wren (1632 to 1723), architect of St Paul's Cathedral, his close friend from Oxford days and partner in the rebuilding of London.
Isaac Newton (1643 to 1727), his great rival. They argued about light from 1672 and about gravity from the 1680s.
Christiaan Huygens (1629 to 1695), the Dutch scientist with whom he fought over who invented the balance spring.
Grace Hooke, his niece, who lived with him as housekeeper and, his diary shows, as his lover in the 1670s.
Edmond Halley (1656 to 1742), the astronomer who carried the gravity question from the coffee house to Newton in 1684.
He grew up through the English Civil War and Cromwell's rule, and the Royal Society was founded in the year Charles II came back to the throne, 1660.
In 1665 the Great Plague killed about a fifth of London's people, and the next year the Great Fire burned much of the city.
London's coffee houses were where scientists, merchants and architects argued and made deals. Hooke went to them almost daily, and his diary records hundreds of visits.
Biology still uses his word 'cell', and every engineering student learns Hooke's law.
For two centuries he was remembered mostly as Newton's bad-tempered rival. Since the 2003 tercentenary of his death, historians have presented him as one of the greatest experimenters of his age.

ps.t: He has been called 'England's Leonardo' for the range of what he did.
ps.why: A modern description, used in popular histories, not a title from his own time.

myths.c: No portrait of Hooke survives because Newton destroyed it.
myths.t: No undoubted portrait survives. The Royal Society's portrait was lost, perhaps when it moved house in 1710 while Newton was its president, but there is no evidence he destroyed it. A painting by Mary Beale of around 1680, the one shown here, has been proposed as Hooke, but this is not proven and has been strongly challenged.

myths.c: Newton stole the inverse square law from Hooke.
myths.t: Hooke suggested the idea and asked the right question in 1679. Others, including Wren and Halley, had guessed it too. Newton was the one who proved that it produces the planets' elliptical orbits.

myths.c: Hooke discovered the cell as we know it.
myths.t: He named the empty boxes he saw in dead cork. The idea that all living things are made of living cells came in the 1830s, from Schleiden and Schwann.

myths.c: Hooke designed buildings that still stand in London.
myths.t: The Monument, which he designed with Wren, still stands near London Bridge, 202 feet tall, the same as its distance from the spot in Pudding Lane where the fire began. Much of his other work has been lost or credited to Wren.
